newsitem.title: LEBANON: MEA counts cost of Israeli blitz.
newsitem.headline: MEA counts cost of Israeli blitz.

text.p: BEIRUT, Oct 7 (REUTER) - Lebanon's Middle East Airlines (MEA) suffered a loss of revenues of up to $15 million due to a 17-day Israeli blitz against Lebanon in April, MEA chairman Khaled Salam was quoted on Monday as saying.
"MEA suffered big losses during 'Operation Grapes of Wrath' last April...the loss reached between $12 to $15 million," Salam told the Beirut daily newspaper Nida'a al-Watan.
"The influence of the Israeli operation went on many months later because it led to the cancellation of many reservations in June from Brazil, Australia and Europe," Salam said.

Israel launched a 17-day blitz on April 11 against pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas, killing some 200 people, mostly civilians, and causing extensive damage estimated by Lebanese officials at $500 million.
Salam put MEA's total net losses at the end of 1995 at $210 million, after operating costs and interest expenses, due to the 1975-90 Lebanese civil war.
He said the company was expected to begin showing a profit in 1998 after the entry into service of new Airbus planes it was leasing to upgrade its ailing 14-plane fleet.

"Experts expect the debts of the company to be settled completely during 1998 when it would be able to achieve some profits from the services of the Airbus planes with which the fleet of the company will be modernized," Salam added.
Salam said last month that MEA has leased four new Airbus planes -- the first of which will arrive at the start of 1997 from Hamburg -- and plans to lease four more.

MEA flourished before the war but the fighting and the devaluation of the Lebanese pound increased its debts and reduced its 150-million-pound capital to $96,000 before shareholders launched an operation to increase it by $225 million last July.

Last month the shareholders agreed to carry out a $100 million debt for equity swap as the first stage of the increase and an additional increase of $125 million will be agreed at a shareholders meeting on October 11.

MEA officials have said that the $125 million will come from cash contribution from shareholders. In the first capital increase, the central bank took up 90 percent of the $100 million in shares, effectively becoming MEA's main shareholder.
